# dsh-plugin-notify

A DeepSeek Harness plugin that shows a **native desktop card whenever the agent
needs you** — becaus

e it is waiting for an answer, or because the task it was
given has finished. It tells you; you answ

for an answer, or because the task it was
given has finished. It tells you; you answer in the chat.
| Question | Permission prompt |
| Two questions, one card | Plan review |
| Task finished | Task failed |
## It notifies; it does not answer

The card has **no answer buttons**. Clicking it brings the chat forward, and the
answer is always gi

as **no answer buttons**. Clicking it brings the chat forward, and the
answer is always given there.

That is a deliberate reversal of an earlier design that answered from the card.
The chat client owns
each pending question through its own waterfall channel:
[代码示例省略，未执行]

An answer delivered out-of-band settles the *request* while leaving the client's
card on screen with

nothing able to settle it — so answering from the card left
the chat asking for an action that had

already been taken. A host plugin cannot
reach into that channel, so it does not answer at all.

The plugin is therefore a **pure observer**: it calls `next()` and returns
whatever the rest of the

waterfall produced, so the chat behaves exactly as it
would without this plugin installed.
### How a card goes away
| You | What happens |

| **Click the card** | Brings the chat forward and dismisses the card. |
| **Click the ✕** | Dismiss

es it without switching to the chat. |
| **Answer in the chat** | The card retires on its own. |
| *
*Nothing** | It stays. A card never times out. |

The auto-close is worth spelling out, because it looks like answering but is not.
The plugin calls `

next()` and returns it untouched; `next()` resolves when the
chat's own answerer settles the request

, so a `.then` on that same promise fires
exactly when the question stops being pending. The plugin

then writes a
`<cardId>.close` marker, and the card's poll picks it up and slides away. The
value re
turned to the waterfall is never altered, which the smoke test asserts.

### Task-finished notifications

There is no service for "the task is done" — the harness records it as a
`turn/end` session event ca
rrying a reason from `TurnEndReasonMap`:
| `reason.kind` | Announced by default | Why |

| `completed` | yes | the normal "done" |
| `error` | yes | a failure matters more than a success |

| `max-tokens` | yes | it stopped early, which is worth knowing |
| `aborted`, `interrupted` | no |

you stopped it yourself |
| `forked` | no | a session fork, not a user-visible task |
| `blocked` |
no | the loop refused to continue; opt in if you want it |
Set `turnEndReasons` to change the set, or `turnEnd: false` to turn all of it off.

The body is the last thing the agent said — almost always the summary of what it
just did — read fro

m the same event stream rather than from the session log, so
[该节后续省略]
## How it works

Both question/approval seams are Cordis **waterfalls**. Waterfalls are dispatched
with an agent scop

e, and `dsh-scope` admits untagged listeners to every
descendant scope, so a single registration obs

erves every agent, subagents
included.

Turn ends are not a waterfall: they are ordinary `session/event` updates, which
the same rule lets t

his plugin observe for every session without knowing which
agents exist.
### Why a PowerShell-drawn card instead of a Windows toast

* The DSH host runs in a **Node child process spawned by the Electron shell**
(`dsh-desktop-host/lib

/index.js`), not in the Electron main process, so
`electron.Notification` is not reachable from a pl

ugin.
* On Windows 11 24H2 the WinRT toast APIs reject unpackaged senders with
`0x80073D54 "The proc

ess has no package identity"` — verified against both the
app's registered AppUserModelID (`com.deep

seek.dsh`) and an explicit process
AUMID. A toast sender would first have to register an AppUserMode

lID and a
Start Menu shortcut.

So the card is a short-lived, hidden `powershell.exe` drawing an ordinary
borderless topmost window

— a rounded `Region` for the corners and
`CS_DROPSHADOW` for the shadow. See `lib/card.cs`.

An earlier version used a **layered window** (`WS_EX_LAYERED` +
`UpdateLayeredWindow`), which is the

only way to get antialiased rounded corners
*and* a genuinely soft shadow. It was replaced after a

long debugging session in
which it appeared never to display — a diagnosis that turned out to rest o

n a
broken screen-capture method (a sandboxed shell cannot composite *any* window, so
both a plain a

nd a layered test window captured as zero pixels). The layered
version may well have been fine; this

one is kept because it is simpler and
demonstrably displays.
## Limitations

- **Windows only** (`os: ["win32"]` in `package.json`). The hook layer is
portable; `lib/card.cs` an

d `lib/popup.ps1` are not.
- **It never answers.** By design — see the top of this file. Answering h

appens
in the chat.
- **Cost per card** is one process start plus an `Add-Type` compile of ~33 KB of

C# (~0.5 s, longer when several cards start at once). Cards are rare, so this
is deliberate: a shor

t-lived helper cannot leak or hang around after a crash.
- **No focus detection.** A card is shown e

ven when the Harness window is already
focused; the host has no reliable "is the user looking at me"

signal. This
applies to turn-end cards too, so every finished turn notifies even while you
are read

ing the chat. Set `turnEnd: false`, or trim `turnEndReasons`, if that
is too chatty.
- **A card stay

s until you click it.** By design. `maxStack` bounds how many can
pile up, and pushed cards count do

k it.** By design. `maxStack` bounds how many can
pile up, and pushed cards count down on their own.
